content:
This site used to run on Docsify — markdown rendered client-side by JS, no build step. Fine for a quick personal page, bad for anything you want search engines to actually read: crawlers that don’t execute JS see an empty shell, and there’s no per-page metadata to speak of.
I wanted something boring instead: static HTML generated at build time, no framework churn, no dependency on a CDN script staying online. Hugo fit — a single binary, no Ruby/Node toolchain to maintain, markdown in, HTML out. I build locally and push the output straight to /docs; no CI pipeline to babysit.
The theme is PaperMod — minimal by default, built-in search, dark/light toggle, and it doesn’t need me to write CSS. Same content model as before (markdown files, some images), just rendered properly this time.

content:
Rolling out AI-assisted development across a 9-person cross-functional team wasn’t about handing everyone a Copilot license and calling it done — most of the gain came from where in the workflow we applied it.
Scaffolding, not judgment. The time savings showed up in boilerplate-heavy work — API endpoint scaffolding, migration files, repetitive test setup, translating a spec into a first-pass implementation. Architecture decisions, service boundaries, and anything touching regulatory logic stayed human-reviewed line by line. The tool is fast at typing; it’s not accountable for a compliance requirement being met.
Parallel workstreams became viable. With less time spent on mechanical implementation, engineers could carry more than one ticket at a time without the usual context-switching tax — a big part of why cycles compressed rather than just each ticket getting marginally faster.
Review discipline had to go up, not down. Faster output raises the cost of a bad review. We kept the same code review bar and, if anything, got stricter about it for AI-assisted PRs — the failure mode isn’t “the code doesn’t compile,” it’s “the code compiles and looks plausible but is subtly wrong,” which is a harder thing to catch on autopilot.
The 2-weeks-to-3-days number is real, but it’s a team-level outcome, not a tooling benchmark — it came from treating the model as a fast first-draft generator inside a review process we didn’t loosen, not from trusting it to make decisions.

content:
ERC-4626 was designed for yield-bearing crypto vaults — deposit an ERC-20, get shares, redeem later at a different exchange rate. The mechanics translate reasonably well to tokenized real-world assets, but a few assumptions in the standard stop holding once the underlying isn’t sitting on-chain.
Redemption isn’t instant. A crypto vault can settle a withdrawal in the same block. An RWA vault backed by a bond or a fund unit is gated by the actual settlement cycle of that asset — T+2, a subscription/redemption window, sometimes a manual custodian step. previewRedeem and maxWithdraw need to reflect that reality rather than assume liquidity is always there, or integrators will build against numbers the vault can’t honor.
Share price isn’t purely on-chain data. For a DeFi vault, totalAssets() is a balance you can read from a contract. For an RWA vault, it depends on a NAV or valuation that comes from off-chain records — administrator statements, custodian confirmations. That valuation has to be pushed on-chain by something accountable, which means the vault’s trust model now includes whoever is authorized to update that number, not just the code.
Compliance sits in the transfer path, not around it. Investor eligibility (accredited status, jurisdiction, KYC/KYB) has to be enforced at transfer time, which usually means wrapping transfer/transferFrom with a compliance check rather than treating the token as a bare ERC-20. ERC-7540 (async deposit/redeem extensions to 4626) helps model the delayed-settlement piece, but the compliance layer is still something you build on top, not something either standard gives you.
None of this is a reason to avoid 4626 for tokenized assets — it’s still the right shape for the share/asset accounting. It’s just not a drop-in; the parts that assume instant, code-only settlement are exactly the parts that need to be replaced with something that reflects how the underlying asset actually settles.
summary:
